subsubtopic: MR. TRUDEAU-REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The reason I ask for this consent of the House is simply because I have a very important meeting with many businessmen from across the country which is scheduled to start at eleven o'clock, and I think it would be very helpful to me and to them if I could be allowed to state my question of privilege now. I understand the House might want to ask me a few questions. I would certainly agree to stay and answer a few of them, but I hope the House will understand that I will not stay for the whole question period as soon as hon. members go on to other matters.
My question of privilege has to do with a very misleading and mischievous headline in the Globe and Mail this morning, and if I had the unanimous consent of the House I would proceed to the matter now.

Of course, the Prime Minister can choose whether or not he would stay for any part of the ordinary question period, but in any event if he is prepared to stay, as I understand he is, for questions on his statement-which I think is important-it should be realized that this transcends the importance of any meeting with any

-and therefore my staff was unable to reach me. However, my staff did look all night for any letter from the former auditor general which might mention bribery, and no such letter was found. We did dig up a letter from the former auditor general to me, dated March 22, 1973, which involves invoicing practices. The letter concerns the invoicing practices of Polymer Corporation.
I took immediate action on this letter from the former Auditor General. It was acknowledged four days after it was dated, and the next day-five days after the date of the letter-I forwarded a letter to the hon. member for West-mount (Mr. Drury), who was then president of the treasury board, asking that he study this matter or make inquiries relating to these invoicing practices. I was not able to reach the hon. member this morning because he is out west, but I do have from his office a copy of my letter to him, on which he wrote on the bottom some words in his handwriting. It says: "Called Morrison, CDC"-"executive vice-president", if I read it correctly-"on March 29", in other words, two days after having received my letter, "and he has undertaken to get Hampson"-who was president of the CDC-"to justify in writing the future policy of Polysar, Polymer, CDC." All this came to my attention within minutes, and we are presently making inquiries of the CDC to find out what action was taken as a result of these requests.
So my question of privilege is essentially one of drawing to the attention of the House the misleading nature of that headline which talks about bribery, whereas there is no mention of that in the letter. I repeat that it talks about invoicing practices, but however that may be viewed and understood, the important point I want to bring to the attention of you, Mr. Speaker, and the House is that I took immediate action and the minister involved took immediate action. As yet we do not know what follow-up was made by the Crown corporations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not in any way to ask questions or to make any point on behalf of the official opposition but, rather, in my role as chairman of the public accounts committee. I think what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has done here this morning

is quite proper and correct. It is an attempt to clear up a very serious allegation against the office of the Prime Minister. I merely want to point out to the House, to the Prime Minister and to the government House leader, that these rather serious allegations have been made by an individual who is not now, but was once, a servant of parliament, the former auditor general.
In those days, as in these days, the auditor general's vehicle of communication, in many ways, with this House was through the public accounts committee. I would suspect that the terms of reference of the current public accounts committee would forbid us to go into this matter, although I am not too sure about that, in that our terms of reference are the current public accounts and the current Auditor General's report on those accounts to this House.
What the former auditor general has said, or is reported as having said, in the article referred to by the right hon. Prime Minister may or may not have reference to current investigations which are going to be undertaken by the public accounts committee. There are things which, in my mind, perhaps at the time should have been reported to the then public accounts committee and not, perhaps, even to the Prime Minister, but that is by the way.
I merely suggest to the Prime Minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that because the public accounts committee is going to be looking at the role of these Crown corporations, and because Polymer is one of these corporations and we might be prevented from asking these questions-and I know the Prime Minister would like to have the matter cleared up-with the House Leader sitting beside him, that together they might come up with terms of reference expanding the public accounts committee. In that way it may be possible to call Mr. Henderson before the committee so that we can perhaps find out if he has been misinterpreted on this whole matter.
I think that is a valid request. I am trying to put it forward in the same tones of sweet reason that we just heard from the Prime Minister. I can see no possible objection to it. It would fit in with what we are trying to do in the public accounts committee, in any event. If we had Mr. Henderson before us, and he continued with these allegations, and perhaps might even be able to provide us with proof, I am sure the Prime Minister himself would like to appear before the committee in the event that the terms of reference were so wide.
Even if the terms of reference are not wide, I am not sure that the public accounts committee could not inquire into this matter. But let us resolve all doubt about it. If the Prime Minister wants to get to the bottom of the allegations, as we do, I am sure he would agree that the terms of reference for that committee should be widened as soon as possible to make sure we can call Mr. Henderson before it.

The Prime Minister says that is clear. It certainly was not clear in his opening statement in which he said he had to go to another meeting.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of points which have to be cleared up, and I hope they can be cleared up later. The first is whether the letter to which the Prime Minister referred is the same letter to which the former auditor general was referring. He makes the very serious statement that he wrote privately to the Prime Minister suggesting that he had information indicating that Canadian Crown corporations were paying bribes to foreign buyers to sell certain products. That is a serious charge.
If there is another letter, I think Mr. Henderson ought to have the opportunity to appear before the public accounts committee, if he is willing to appear, to produce such a letter. Certainly, the Prime Minister has the obligation to have his staff search further to see whether such letter exists. The second thing we ought to know is whether the invoices are being tabled and whether they deal with any company or Crown corporation other than the CDC, which is apparently the only company regarding which Mr. Drury, who was then president of the treasury board, made any inquiries. That matter should be cleared up.
I support the suggestion made, that the terms of reference of the public accounts committee should be widened. That committee has not yet sat. The terms of reference will be, as I understand them, the public accounts and the Auditor General's report. But the matters to which Mr. Maxwell Henderson refers, of course, have much wider scope and cover a different period of time. Therefore, I think the public accounts committee, on the government's initiative-and there will have to be a motion in the House-should be given the widest possible latitude in order to allow Mr. Henderson to appear, to allow the Prime Minister to appear, to ascertain whether there is a letter other than that which the Prime Minister tabled this morning, and to find out whether Mr. Henderson has any substantial evidence to corroborate the statements he makes when he claims that he wrote to the Prime Minister saying that he had information which led him to believe that certain Canadian Crown corporations were using bribes.
Oral Questions
I think this matter cannot be settled simply by a statement by the Prime Minister. We are prepared to accept the statement that this is the only correspondence he can find, but it seems to me, in view of the seriousness of the charge and in view of the person from whom it comes, that this matter ought to have very thorough investigation by the public accounts committee, on the basis of widened terms of reference, so that there will not be any nit-picking as to whether that committee has full authority to go back to some period in time in order to look into this matter and related matters regarding agents who have been used by Crown corporations and have submitted accounts which have been called in question, not just by Mr. Maxwell Henderson but by the present Auditor General.

I have tabled the documents that I have in my possession. Your Honour will realize that I was only apprised of this matter a couple of hours ago. We got all the information we have at this time. Questions about other papers or other matters are, as far as I am concerned, hypothetical.
I want to make it clear that in the former Auditor General's letter he only refers to one company, Polymer. Presumably because Polymer was acquired by the CDC, he also mentions the CDC, saying that he sent a copy of this letter to Mr. Rush, president of Polymer and Mr. Hampson chairman of the board of the CDC. It is possible they will have further documents in which the House might be interested. I have no knowledge of them.
As far as the Public Accounts committee is concerned, if I understand the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, he would like to know from the former Auditor General why he did not apprise parliament of this rather than writing to me privately. If I could go on and answer the point raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, he asked me if there is any other letter. I thought I had answered that in my opening statement. I said that my staff looked all night for any letter from Mr. Henderson which might mention bribes and they found none. It was in order to be as forthcoming as possible with the House that I produced this letter which may have been the one he had in mind. If that is it, I think the House will agree that the press story was very mischievous and misleading indeed.
If there is another letter, I have challenged Mr. Henderson to produce it. I was asked about this when I came into the

Parliament Buildings this morning. I said that I had no recollection of any letter mentioning bribes. If there is one, we have not found it. Perhaps Mr. Henderson can produce it, if it exists.

This question, Mr. Speaker, along with the previous one, obviously brings into debate the question whether Crown corporations should be at arm's length from the government or whether we should be attempting to manage their affairs, and whether the Auditor General of this parliament should also be Auditor General of Crown corporations which parliament created at arm's length from the government. This question can be discussed and debated. I have no particular desire to have one answer or the other. subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS BY FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL-ACTION TO HAVE POLYMER PRACTICE CHANGED
speechtext:
Assuming that the letter which the Prime Minister has tabled is the only letter he received from Mr. Henderson, and this is something which Mr. Henderson himself will have to divulge, even this letter dated March 22, 1973 did endeavour to draw to the attention of the Prime Minister a serious situation concerning Polymer and its dealings with a Swiss subsidiary, Polysar International SA. Perhaps I might quote a sentence from the letter which sums it up.
Briefly, this arises from the subsidiary's practice of invoicing certain European customers by agreement at inflated prices with the difference being remitted to the customer or their representatives in cash in Switzerland or placed in numbered Swiss bank accounts as directed.
The letter then goes on to say that by doing this the customer was able to dodge the tax collector in his own country to the tune of some $2 million. This was a serious situation to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister more than two years ago. The Prime Minister referred the matter to the minister who was President of the Treasury Board at that time. The President of the Treasury Board merely scrawled a

November 26, 1976
Oral Questions
notation which said "Called Morrison (CDC Executive VP)"-I assume that stands for Vice-President-"March 29; he has undertaken to get Hampson to justify in writing the future policy of Polysar, Polymer, CDC." It is just signed "D"-I assume it stands for Drury.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Prime Minister, first of all, did he get an undertaking from Mr. Hampson as to future policy? If so, will he table that document? Second, did he get any investigation into why Polymer was really compounding a felony by allowing its subsidiary to use closed Swiss bank accounts to dodge tax responsibilities in the customer's country? This is a pretty nefarious practice and it was drawn to the attention of the government three years ago last March.

There is nothing in this letter which uses that kind of word at all. The Auditor General does not seem to be concerned with the illegality, or indeed even the immorality, of any of these practices; he is concerned with a contingent liability.

subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS BY FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL-ACTION TO HAVE POLYMER PRACTICE CHANGED
speechtext: How do you feel about this?

subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS BY FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL-ACTION TO HAVE POLYMER PRACTICE CHANGED
speechtext:
The facts as I know them do not permit me to know of any felony or any impropriety. If hon. members look at my letter to Mr. Drury, they will see I say on page 2:
While there may be no strict breach of law involved in the action that is referred to (I do not know whether that is the case or not), and while the government may not have complete control or direct responsibilityand so on. So I am interested in these questions too, but obviously they are not the aspects which concern the Auditor General.

In so far as his allegations or his statements are concerned, he does refer to tax liabilities and foreign exchange control regulations where they exist. He makes no judgment on this matter either, because I think quite properly he takes the point of view that it is not for him to see if other countries are collecting their taxes in the way they should. He just wants to make sure that our own accounting practices are correct and that they do not bring into account contingent liabilities which might cause us problems. So I repeat to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, as I did to the opposition House leader, that it would be very misleading and damaging now to read into this letter moral insinuations and criminal liabilities, and I object to that very strongly.

subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS BY FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL-ACTION TO HAVE POLYMER PRACTICE CHANGED
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister knows perfectly well that when I spoke of any felony it was by a subsidiary that was apparently trying to use certain techniques to evade its customer's tax responsibilities in whatever country it was located. What I am interested in is whether a Canadian Crown corporation was a party to such attempted deceit. I should like to ask the Prime Minister, first, whether he condones a Canadian Crown corporation participating in that kind of practice; and secondly, why after more than three years has the Prime Minister not asked for some assurance that such a practice has been discontinued? Has the Prime Minister received any such assurance, will he undertake to get such assurance, and why has it taken so long to look into the matter, or does the Prime Minister not think it is serious?

subsubtopic: ALLEGATIONS BY FORMER AUDITOR GENERAL-ACTION TO HAVE POLYMER PRACTICE CHANGED

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to resume debate on Bill C-19 I would refer to my remarks of last night when I said there is a shocking lack of planning by this government, particularly in the Department of Transport. There are heavy lay-offs in the steel industry, but no plans are advanced on how to assist the regions faced with these lay-offs -which come as a result of lack of orders from railway companies and the government's neglect to plan for building more boxcars and railway facilities. Those of us who have an interest in transportation and the railways know there is a dire need for new equipment.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said that he wants this bill passed. Last night I said that we on this side are prepared to pass it as long as the government makes some serious effort to cut waste and inefficiency and the downright extravagance of their ways. There has been a continuous decline in the amount of money spent on a research and development; there has been some fancy bookkeeping, but there has been no plan or goal set for Canada.
A recent federal conference on residence and homes which took place in Vancouver was told that the increased cost of homes contributed greatly to the increased cost of living in Canada. The director general of Canada's participation in Habitat has said that within the next 25 years Canada will have to build more residences, more industrial facilities, more hospitals, more transportation, more power stations and more
Restraint of Government Expenditures urban utilities than were built in the last 108 years in this country. A massive job lies ahead of us, Mr. Speaker. We see this government spending more and more money, but it has no direct goal. It attempts to control inflation by controlling the money supply, but does not attempt to control the growth of government expenditures in any serious way.
Recently, the OECD countries suggested that the western world would have a growth rate of 3.5 per cent or 4 per cent. In bringing down his budget, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said that government expenditures would not grow any faster than the gross national product. Mr. Speaker, government expenditures are growing at a rate twice the rate of the gross national product, and the OECD projects it will continue to double for all of 1977.
I quote the OECD countries to try to project an unbiased point of view so that the government can be serious about what it intends to do with regard to controlling expenditures and developing the country. The OECD ranked Canada tenth and last on performance and technological innovation. We have a great country, great wealth, the people are highly educated, yet we rank last in the use of our knowledge and education for bettering conditions in this country. We rank second to last in the proportion of our work force employed in the secondary manufacturing industry. There is a high degree of industrial development throughout much of central Canada and Atlantic Canada, but there is no real effort to develop a science policy or a research and development policy to aid our manufacturing industries to compete with other trading nations.
The OECD stated that we had the largest trade deficit in 1975 of most of the industrial countries in the western world, and that we had a huge trade deficit in management and engineering-oriented services. In the old days that was called a brain drain. There are many reasons why we have had such a massive brain drain, Mr. Speaker, as well as a money drain. We have had a cutback in research and development and a curtailment in science policy. This is pointed out in a letter which I received from the Agricultural Institute of Canada, which I am sure most hon. members have received. The letter dated November 8, 1976, begins:
A statement highlighting the worsening situation of agricultural research and development in Canada is enclosed. It has been prepared by the Agricultural Institute of Canada.
Bill C-19 has much to do with agriculture, Mr. Speaker, and, of course, one of the main means of balancing our payments in this country is through the sale of food products. There has been a slight surplus of agricultural exports over imports, but we could have done much better. Our neighbour to the south has taken two steps in order to attain a balance of payments. They have sold armaments and food. We are not in the business of selling armaments, but we can, and should, sell more agricultural products. We should be encouraging more agricultural production than we can consume ourselves, but this government has deliberately discouraged this. In the end, it will have a serious effect on our balance of payments.
About 7 per cent of the land area of Canada is suitable for agricultural production, yet last year we were able to export

November 26, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures only in the neighbourhood of $3.9 billion in agricultural products. Imports of every one of the major staple foods produced in Canada was increased, however. Imports of beef were increased by about 60 per cent, and hogs and pork by about 110 per cent. Three or four of our provinces are big producers of apples, yet there was an increase of 60 per cent in the apples that came into Canada last year. We are not doing enough with this great country, Mr. Speaker. The Agricultural Institute of Canada suggests that we are cutting back on research and experimentation in a great variety of goods.
It is not enough that Bill C-19 suggests that the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act be extended for another year. We have to do much more than that. The position paper of the Agricultural Institute of Canada reads:
There is an intellectual resource of scientifically trained academics with research interests in the 11 facilities of agriculture and veterinary science at Canadian universities. Some provincial governments and agricultural industries also have active agricultural research and development programs.
They go on to suggest that not enough money is allocated to research and development programs, that the federal government has cut back spending on research at universities, and they quote the 1970 special Senate committee report on science policy which said that there should be increased spending on research and development related to the growth of the gross national product. As our gross national product rises, so should our ability to spend money on science, research and development. This government has failed in this regard. It has done little to enable this country to extricate itself, through increased production, from its dilemma.
I now turn to the handling of our finances. Frankly, I do not think this bill will save money. Yesterday, for the first time in a long time, the exchange rate for the Canadian dollar dipped below the value of the American dollar. Many pundits, whom I do not rank highly as economists or experts, attribute the decline in the value of the Canadian dollar to the result of the recent vote in Quebec. I do not accept that view. I think the western world, particularly the United States, realizes that our competitive position vis-a-vis our competitor to the south, Germany, Japan, and other countries, has deteriorated. Our costs are higher.
We may boast of our wage and price controls and our Anti-Inflation Board, but the fact remains that production costs are higher in this country. In nearly every economic sector, including the tourist industry, with respect to the production of manufactured goods, agriculture, and lumber products, our costs of production are higher. Therefore, our competitive position is not as good as that of our trading partners and our dollar has begun to decline. Unless the government enables us to improve our competitive position, allows us to spend more money on research and development, and encourages the use of innovative, new technology, we shall remain in an inferior position relative to our major competitors and our dollar will continue its downward slide.
If our dollar continues to go down, it will be an indication that our government is not managing this country's economy
(Mr. Horner.]
as well as the governments of our major competitors in the western world are managing their economies. In my opinion, this government has failed miserably in the management of our economy. By maintaining high interest rates it has encouraged the importation of huge amounts of foreign investment, which kept the value of our dollar slightly above that of the American dollar. Unfortunately, high interest rates contribute to our inability to compete with our neighbours. I say this because industry in Canada must pay up to 4 per cent or 5 per cent more for capital with which to enlarge and modernize productive capacity than industry pays south of the border. These higher interest rates represent an added cost of doing business in Canada, which must be passed on to the consumer and so increases the price of goods produced in Canada.
The old argument that high interest rates curtail inflation is questionable, to say the least. In this country much business is carried on with borrowed money, and high interest rates merely force up the cost of doing business. The government's deliberate insistence on keeping interest rates in Canada 4 per cent above those in the United States has created severe hardship and has damaged the productive capacity of many industries, including the agricultural industry, which could help greatly to improve our balance of payments.
What I have said will show you what I think of this particular bill, Mr. Speaker. I have nothing but contempt for it, for it shows that the government has no direction, no plan and no goal. It is not even motivated to bringing this country back on track, to making it more competitive in the western world and providing jobs for the many Canadians seeking work. Also, Mr. Speaker, many Canadians will seek work this winter. This legislation does nothing for them.
I now come to the Auditor General's report. When one examines the Auditor General's report and compares it with this legislation, one sees that the two are incompatible. The Auditor General says that he sees all kinds of inequities in the government's accounting system; that based on studies of the system of departments, agencies and Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General it is evident that the financial management and control of the government of Canada is grossly inadequate.
Mr. Speaker, the members of this House are merely representatives of the shareholders of a great company, the government of Canada. If the auditor of any business said that the control of spending of the management team was grossly inadequate-and the government is really nothing but a group of executives managing this great company-the shareholders would call a very important meeting to set up a better accounting system for the executives of the company.
The statement by the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), that a royal commission is to be set up in order to study the system whereby the government's books are audited, just was not good enough. Why did the government not implement the 32 recommendations made by the Auditor General? The appointment of a comptroller general who would be a check on the Treasury Board and the spending of the executive I suggest would in no way infringe

upon the parliamentary process. Treasury Board has the obligation and responsibility to allocate resources. The Auditor General has the responsibility of seeing whether there is excessive waste in the money allocated for resource development or regional development by the Treasury Board.
I have read of the problems in the Department of Transport. In fact, I read a very revealing statement. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) said that no additional airports would be built in Canada without consulting the airlines. That is an admission that when Mirabel was built, the airlines were not consulted with regard to the kind of terminal facilities they wanted. When talking to the former president of Air Canada, he informed me that he was not consulted about the public transit vehicles used between the terminal and the airport. In fact, when he was told what the system would be at Mirabel, he informed the government that it was a very costly and wasteful system. He informed them that only one airport, the Dallas airport, used that system and it was heavily subsidized. The government went ahead with it despite the advice of the president of Air Canada. In addition, CP Air and the other airlines were not consulted.
There was the same kind of situation when the new airport was built at Calgary. Time Airlines, one of the few airlines which made a profit last year and which is not subsidized by the government, said that the Department of Transport was building such a fancy terminal in Calgary, at such an exorbitant cost, that they doubted they would be able to use it. They said that the cost of flying into that airport would be increased so much that it would severely handicap them in their ability to balance their books.
We can also look at the airports at Edmonton and Winnipeg. The users, the airlines, were not consulted.
Terminal two is another prime example of the allocation of resources by Treasury Board. The Auditor General was not given the opportunity to check on the correct allocation of those funds. Terminal two was to be a terminal for the international carriers. However, when the international carriers saw it, they refused to move into it. Air Canada was forced to move into it and the international carriers stayed in terminal one. That is another example of gross mismanagement of the taxpayers' money.
Many members of parliament and the press have been making hay with regard to the Minister of Transport's abuse of the public trust placed in him, with his exorbitant travelling costs. He stated in all seriousness that he had to fly to Calgary a year ago for the Grey Cup game in order to represent the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde). I do not know why the Minister of National Health and Welfare had to be represented at the Grey Cup game. The Prime Minister was there. Could he not have represented him? It would not then have been necessary to spend $8,080 to fly the Minister of Transport to the Grey Cup game. I do not want to discourage attendance at this Sunday's Grey Cup game, but I hope the Minister of Transport does not go.

The Prime Minister should relieve him of that excessive work by appointing another member from Saskatchewan to take over the job as minister of transport. In that way the minister and his wife could get back to looking after their seven children.
In yesterday's Ottawa Citizen, the wife of the Prime Minister was quoted on what she had to say about politicians. Speaking in Peterborough, she stated that she was concerned about the honesty of politicians, and assured the ladies present that her husband was very honest. She said:

I agree. She went on to say:

I hope she is right there, too, and that the poor politicians will be weeded out. She has the ear of the Prime Minister. She could be very influential in weeding them out before an election. She could assist the Prime Minister in weeding out a few of his careless ministers who are abusing the public trust. The Minister of Transport has fouled up almost everything he has touched-the air traffic controllers, the car rental systems I spoke about last night, and allocating $30 million to CPR which did not know what kind of experiment the department wanted carried out.

November 26, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
Last evening members of the CTC appeared before the committee. I suggested to them that they had a good deal of expertise in passenger traffic, having travelled across Canada to study the question. I asked whether they were consulted before the government allocated $30 million for an experimental passenger train as to what kind of experiment should be carried out. They said they were not consulted at all.
Representatives of the CPR the recipient of the $30 million, informed me and other people interested in transportation that if the government wanted to carry out an experiment on rail passenger traffic, that experiment should be carried out between Ottawa and Montreal. They stated there was good track for the full distance between Ottawa and Montreal. They could change a few curvatures and speed up the train on that track to 125 m.p.h., if that is the speed at which the department wants it to travel. But for one reason or another the experiment is not to take place on the track most suitable for it, because the CPR was not sufficiently consulted.
The minister and his department had it in the back of their minds all along where that money was to be spent. They are going to improve a 25-mile stretch of the track between Quebec City and Montreal. The train will travel at 125 m.p.h. for 25 miles, after which it will slow down to 60 m.p.h. or 70 m.p.h. This doesn't make much sense to me, and it will not make much sense to the travelling public. It would have made a lot more sense if they had spent the money to improve the track all the way from Ottawa to Montreal, not too great a distance to travel conveniently by train. Then they would have known whether or not the appeal of a good railway passenger service can still attract customers. To my mind, this decision is one more example of the incompetence of the Minister of Transport. Now we have evidence of his abusive use of government aircraft. On one occasion the minister flew from Ottawa to Toronto at a cost to the taxpayers of $8,027. He flew by Viscount, and I suppose the bill was larger because he left the Viscount parked in Toronto for three or four days. If it had been flown back empty, it would not have cost the taxpayers so much money. I suppose the minister was making an important decision, one which took him four or five days to arrive at.

I

understand that one of them served at one time in the Liberal administration in Saskatchewan; he was minister of education, so he knows something about running a department. Maybe his respect for the public trust would be a whole lot better than that of the present minister.
Mr. Speaker, I have given the House some idea of my feelings about Bill C-19. I hope many Liberal members become involved in the debate on this subject because they, too, must demonstrate clearly to their voters that they are concerned about waste of money in government. They do not have to single out any particular minister if they do not wish to do so. They can simply express the concern which their constituents have been expressing to them. There is nobody in Canada who has not heard about "Lang Air" or who does not know about Otto's nanny. People are writing to their members, and backbenchers on the Liberal side should be on their feet demonstrating their concern because the government is not doing enough to curtail the extravagance and waste, evidence of which we find in the report of the Auditor General, in returns to questions on the order paper, and in the press.
All this is causing difficulty at home for every Liberal backbencher. They should be advising the government that they are not going to put up with it for ever. The Prime Minister has an obligation to shake up the cabinet in a way which would help Canada and which might even be beneficial to the Liberal party.

speechtext:
I will remind the hon. member opposite that perhaps I could give him some information which the government might find constructive, but it is difficult to say anything when there is a foghorn on the other side. That is the trouble we sometime have in some of the maritime ports in foggy weather but we are used to it. In any event, it appears that
November 26, 1976

Treasury Board practices are being badly circumvented in certain respects in Statistics Canada, and this is of relevance in any debate on a restraint bill, whether it is the one before the House or any other such bill.
I have interesting information which was conveyed to me, and which I would like to convey to the House, about some of the practices which should be, if not amended at least looked at very closely by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). Computer systems people, according to my informant, were hired by the system development division in 1972. They are hired for a certain number of days or months, and when the period expires and there is more money available, the contract is extended, again for a certain number of days. In the spring of 1975, system development division employees at Statistics Canada numbered approximately 170 permanent people and 40 to 45 contractors.
All these contractors received consultants fees and were used as part-time help. Not one of the contracts was for the performance of a certain well-defined task or the completion of a project for an agreed upon fee. These contracts remove any risk of loss for the contracting firm; the only party running the risk of loss is Statistics Canada which is, of course, indirectly the government of Canada, a matter which I would think would be of some concern to those opposite who are really interested in saving money, and to the people of Canada. Contract personnel are used as part-time help. They have integrated into the operation and they report to Statistics Canada supervisors. Except for the remuneration, they are treated as employees. There have been instances of contract personnel having participated in performance appraisals of junior Statistics Canada personnel. Some contractors have spent years in Statistics Canada.
I have information on one contractor, whose name I will give to the minister rather than name him in the House, who has been with Statistics Canada since 1973. He is independent and each year his income has been higher than that of the division's director. He does work that could be done by a permanent employee, I am informed, at a salary of approximately $18,000. This type of situation is something with which I hope the government will concern itself in the context of restraint. None of these contractors is doing work that could not be done just as well by permanent staff.
One other matter that is causing concern and which has been brought up before-again I will give the specific instance and give the name to the minister later-concerns an employee who joined Statistics Canada in 1972. He went to England shortly thereafter for a conference and returned, together with his family, at government expense. He studied in England during which time he received two-thirds of his salary. He returned in September of this year, and a collective agreement for his group calls for 50 per cent of his salary during his study leave. These types of instances are very relevant. There are such instances as the excessive use of government aircraft or business incompetence and they bear directly on the honesty and competence of this government. If this is not a good time
Restraint of Government Expenditures to mention such instances within the context of Bill C-19 and this debate, then I do not know what is.
Now I should like to move to another topic about which I have great concern, and I want to assure you, sir, that it, too, is related strictly to the expenditure of the taxpayers' money. It relates to the Department of Labour. As I understand it, the background of this matter is that the government is at present attempting to induce the CLC to be more co-operative. They are planning to advance this group a considerable sum of money, millions of dollars perhaps, to set up a centre of learning here in Ottawa and possibly regional centres in various provinces. As I said, the main centre is reported as going to he established in Ottawa. A considerable sum of money will be involved, it appears.
I should like to pose some questions today which I hope the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) will consider and answer. As I understand it, the deal has already been made and it is just a question of how much money has been involved. For example, I should like to know if the CLC has been given assurances by the Minister of Labour that the funds will be received by them, and on what basis. If they are for setting up a labour college for educational purposes, I think this would be constructive in certain circumstances, provided the provinces were consulted, because we are now looking into a question of provincial jurisdiction, provided there is some co-operative effort so that this will be truly an institute of learning, and there will not only be an opportunity to train shop stewards but also foremen so that they can work toward better labour and management relations in this country, not in a unilateral way.
Already the government has been giving money-and I commend them for it-to a labour college which is part of McGill university. If this type of arrangement is going to be carried on a joint federal-provincial basis, then I think the minister should make a statement on motions before he goes any further with this, to tell us what the province's view is and not make any mistakes which he will have to later correct.
The minister and the deputy minister have held meetings across this country for anyone who cared to attend, and in some areas there were very few people, apart from their own staffs, who attended, which says something about the dialogue which exists between labour, government and management in this country at present. I would like to know whether this latest initiative taken by the Minister of Labour is based on the traditional tripartite approach which is equitable and which involves government, management and labour, or whether it is done on a unilateral basis which does not, as is the case in many government policies, take into account the wishes and the needs of other concerned parties. I ask the Minister of Labour: on what basis is, government proposing this payment to labour, and will it be matched with CLC contributions? Will it be tied in with provincial initiatives or matching grants? What will the curriculum be? What do the provinces think and, last but just as important, what will it cost?

November 26, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
I would say at this time that the government of Canada must realize that as an alternative to handing out several million dollars there should be more incentives to encourage labour and management to enter into joint ventures, and to educate not just certain narrow occupations within the labour movement but to bring in representatives from management as well, so there can be a joint effort toward some sort of jurisprudence that will improve the terrible record in the country in recent years which has cost us so much in productivity and has damaged our autonomy.
The government should keep in mind that under the BNA Act the only labour relations fully under federal jurisdiction, in any event, are federal works and undertakings as specifically referred to in section 2 of the Canada Labour Code, and that if the government starts taking unilateral action in taking initiatives with only one partner of the tripartite arrangement-of which it professes to be fond and which 1 think is the proper approach-then perhaps it will do more harm than good.
Referring again to the situation which is troubling the country so far as the report of the Auditor General is concerned, until such time as we get some initiative from the government which can be meaningfully interpreted as a genuine example of trying to save this country money and to live within our means, we are not going to get very far in trying to establish public confidence. The present situation involving the use of public property by ministers in a very casual way, and the government's persistent ignoring of economies which have been put before it either by the opposition or by other wellmeaning sectors of society, is not causing this country to advance as it should in the community of nations.
It has been said in this House in the last couple of days that the various economic indices show that the country is sliding further down on the relative scale of prosperity of western industrialized nations, and that is certainly very evident to anyone who wishes to look at the facts. It is also very clear that the government is getting rather anxious-and I cannot blame it-to have the opposition parties finish with the bill we are discussing. The only difficulty is that this is one of the few forums the opposition has had in recent years to discuss, in a comprehensive way, some of the problems which have frustrated us and some of the facts which must be brought forward for the good of parliament and for the good of the people of Canada.
It has been said before-but I do not think it can be said too many times-that in recent years the executive branch of government has taken unto itself all the prerogatives which are involved in looking after the nation's finances. Parliamentary committees and individual members have no opportunity to examine the estimates in a meaningful way, and when we get a bill such as this before us for our consideration we are provided with an opportunity to suggest to the government certain things it ought to do. Judging by the sensitivity opposite, the government does not want to hear. That is part of the problem;

the government does not wish to listen to constructive suggestions. It is not interested in receiving information, and when it does receive information it is very reluctant to act on it.
Anyone who wants to check the records knows, for example, that it was some time in 1972 that the then minister of transport said he was fully aware that things had to be done to expedite transportation in this country, that he wanted to do something to amend the Railway Act-which is what we are doing in this bill-and that he wanted to do something to take Air Canada away from the control of the CNR. Here we are heading into 1977, many months after a commission of inquiry headed by Mr. Justice Estey, who recommended some of the same things, and they are still not accomplished.
The response of the government to suggestions that things ought to be done is to trot out, in a moment of frantic haste, a royal commission which, however admirable, is certainly not the type of instrument to be used to bring about a quick solution to some of the pressing financial problems facing the country at this time.
Then as a final insult, as it were, to the intelligence of this nation, the Prime Minister came into the House of Commons and tried to tell us that letters such as the one he tabled today, and non-letters such as the one he tabled yesterday, are not to be taken too seriously and that on the face of it there is nothing wrong with acquiescing to the request of a foreign customer to put money into a Swiss bank account, which by the very essence of reading it any person with any common sense would know is not a proper thing to do under the circumstances.
In conclusion, I want to say that until such time as we in this country are prepared to take some stand on the payment of bribes-not necessarily just internationally-we, as parliamentarians, are going to continue to suffer loss of esteem in the eyes of our people, particularly in the field of foreign aid. This government ought to be informed, and inform the nations of the world and its own people that if we have to indulge in the practice of giving bribes in order to be in a position to be able to assist needy people in foreign nations, and if we have to do this by virtue of paying bribes to the people responsible, in many cases, that situation existing, that sort of foreign aid is a type of perversion and should not be given in any event.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill we are discussing is purported to be for the restraining of the expenditures of government so as in some measure to reduce inflationary pressures in Canada. I doubt if one-tenth of 1 per cent of the people of this country do not support that principle. The question, then, is: why are we in the official opposition taking such strong exception to this bill? We are not opposed to its purpose; what we are opposed to is the list of things which have been proposed to use, as whipping boys, to bring down costs.
When I spoke on this matter on November 16 I took violent exception to the attack on the fundamental foundation of federalism. When we formed our country, we made an agreement with the Atlantic provinces-there were four colonies at
November 26, 1976

that time-that if they joined this union we would maintain connections between us. At that time of our history that meant, primarily, railways. It also included shipping. Every administration to this date has maintained that pledge, and yet we find sneaked into this bill, under the pretence of saving money, that we should reduce or get rid of that particular agreement. I referred to this clause before. It is clause 15 and it proposes to repeal section 272 of the Railway Act. Whenever a government breaks an agreement which is 109 years old, that should be done here with a specific bill and a statute to follow it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
What irritates hon. members of the opposition and, I trust, the people of Canada is that the amount of money involved at this stage is very small, $11 million, yet this government would destroy a solemn agreement between independent colonies of the Crown who wanted to join together at that time into a sovereign nation, and that agreement is being broken with the excuse that the government wants to save $11 million. Then right in the middle of the debate, when we are supposed to be discussing attempts to restrain expenditures of the government, every day, every hour and every minute brings a new example of some extravagance by the government or some case where the government is ignoring and refusing to take action on the recommendations of the Auditor General, who reports to parliament. How can we be blamed for saying that this bill is nothing but a posturing device so that the government need not do anything about the real causes of waste in government? I do not want to speak too long, but I want to make it abundantly clear that we have to grapple with the fact of what the issue is, and this, I repeat, is the issue.
When I spoke on November 16, I was outlining the same thoughts as I have been today about this type of attitude. At page 1029 of Hansard I said the following:
If the government was elected to make its own decisions, there could be an argument for it. The truth is that this government does not run the country. The country is run by a small group of civil servants who seize the decision-making powers in each major department and run the country.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: They are neither civil nor servile.

speechtext:
They know best and they tell ministers what to say and what to do. I ask all westerners, all people from Quebec and the Atlantic provinces-
So it goes on, Mr. Speaker. That is what has been demonstrated in the last two weeks. We have the Auditor General's report which bears on the important question of running government and keeping down costs. This is the material that comes in and takes precedence; this is the main report we have from the servant of parliament, the Auditor General. I should like to remind the House of what we have heard so many times before-and I want to put this on the record so there will be no question when anyone reads my speech-of the type of evidence we have before us. This is the view of the Auditor
Restraint of Government Expenditures General in his most recent report as set out in the Conspectus at page 3:	_
I am deeply concerned that, on the evidence of the two-year examination carried out by the audit office, parliament-and indeed the government-has lost or is close to losing effective control of the public purse.
That question has been asked in this House a dozen times in the last week. The significance is that it raises the question of who is responsible. I know that we in parliament, in our urge to get efficiency eight years ago, brought in new rules that took control of the estimates out of parliament. That question will have to be resolved by parliament.
I wonder if we could not track down evidence in respect of the matter I cited in my speech of over a week ago. I refer to the Glassco commission report in this regard. Last spring, when speaking on this matter, I pointed out that the Glassco royal commission had been set up by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) because as a government we were concerned about the efficient administration of the government.
Sometimes you have the impression that you do not have too much say in the running of government. We set up the Glassco commission to make recommendations to us, or whoever followed us, on how we should tighten control and accountability of government agencies, of government and the civil service. The commission reported in 1962. One of the recommendations was that we should raise the salaries or incomes of senior civil servants to a level equal to that obtained in any form of business across Canada, thereby enabling us to draw on the best men in the country to head our departments and agencies. In return for a salary to equal the best in private business, we expected such competence from those civil servants that would match the competence in private enterprise. We expected from them that if they were not competent, they would be held accountable for their actions.
Accountability is a nice word that has been flung around this House during the past week, but it really comes down to the question of what happens to a senior minister or deputy minister who has this income and makes a mess of what he is doing: he lets expenses get out of control, money is spent, bribes are given, millions are spent and we get into a deficit position on the budget-what happens to hold that minister or deputy minister accountable?
There is only one test of accountability: either the man is dismissed or is put out to hard labour for a number of years. Last spring I suggested that he should be put on a pig farm in Saskatchewan. Until we as a government are prepared to hold responsible the men that we appoint to run our departments efficiently, and until we are prepared to punish those who fail to do the job, we have not honoured the recommendation of the Glassco commission, which was to raise their salaries and then hold them accountable. How many senior civil servants have been dismissed in the 15 years since the Glassco commission report? The only people who are fired around here are ministers. Let me develop why that is so and give the evidence, Mr. Speaker.

November 26, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures I turn now to page 10 of the Conspectus, where it comments on who runs the government. I think I know why the Auditor General brought this in. He knows as well as I do that the real bosses around here are not the front benches; the real bosses are that small group who have taken control of a few key departments and agencies. They run this government. After recommending the appointment of a comptroller, the Auditor General says, at page 10:
But there appears to be an important difference of opinion with respect to the basic recommended actions I consider essential to correct the situation about which I am so seriously concerned. This difference was evident in several of the hearings of the public accounts committee during March and April, 1976. Excerpts from two hearings of the public accounts committee are relevant. The first is a statement by the Secretary of the Treasury Board at a hearing on March 18, 1976:
The Treasury Board is the chief financial office of the government of Canada. I happen to serve as deputy minister of the Treasury Board, and I have a responsibility, delegated by my minister to me, to carry out those functions, administrative functions, relative to that task. But the Treasury Board is, to use an analogy, the chief financial office represented here.
Here we have a senior civil servant saying, "I am the chief financial officer of the Treasury Board", which is the chief financial office, and telling the committee and parliamentarians who the boss is. He goes on:
A committee member asked the following question:
.. I think this is an important exchange. When you say the Treasury Board is the chief financial office, I wonder if adequate consideration has been given to pinpointing an individual just so we can talk in normal business language?" To which the Secretary of the Treasury Board replied:
"Mr. Chairman, it may seem satisfying to do that but I have to deal with reality in the sense that the Treasury Board is the group responsible in the government of Canada for the finances of the government of Canada, and I will not qualify that statement.
However, then one comes to the question: How does the Treasury Board discharge that responsibility? It does so by appointing a Secretary of the Treasury Board and I am responsible to them for that function.
So the second point is-I have to put it in my own terminology because I think it is correct in terms of parliamentary language-that I have simply a delegated responsibility and I am not independent of the government of Canada. I am the public servant."
There is the boss, Mr. Speaker. The report continues:
Another member asked:
"Do you not feel there should be a chief financial officer?"
The Secretary of the Treasury Board replied as follows:
"No, sir, I believe a government governs and the government is responsible for doing so and is accountable to the country and it must discharge that responsibility.
I say that very directly."
There you have, in cold terms, the attitude and words of a senior civil servant telling members of parliament on that committee just who runs this country. When the Auditor General, our servant of parliament, comes out and lists all these terrible things that have happened, the government stands up and parrots the words of this civil servant. Why do we have a Prime Minister sitting here? Why does the representative of the Treasury Board sit here? That minister is supposed to speak for all Canadians. Why, then, did he stand up and speak those words I have quoted?

This matter did not arise only in committee. On May 17 the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) asked the following question in the House, as recorded on page 11 of the Conspectus of the Auditor General's report:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the President of the Treasury Board. In view of the recommendation implied by the Auditor General in his report for the year ended March 31, 1975, and later enunciated by him before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, would the minister give very careful consideration to the establishment of the position of chief financial officer within the framework of the public service of Canada to have express responsibility for overseeing matters relating to the adequacy of financial accounting and control measures over the some $40 billion of annual revenues and expenditures involved in the current operations of the government?
The then minister replied, in part:
Mr. Speaker... I am prepared to consider it favourably. There is a problem of organization within the government. We strongly intend to establish the required mechanisms to the satisfaction of the Auditor General, and I think that with respect to this particular matter, the Treasury Board and the Auditor General will finally find a common ground.
The minister who spoke those words sits in this House today. Last spring he was in favour of the idea raised in the question of the hon. member; but now, when the chips are down, the present minister can only stand in this House and repeat the words of the Secretary of the Treasury Board. The government has changed its mind. The minister's boss has spoken. What is the situation? The government has just been exposed to one of the most scathing indictments in the history of this nation. An idea which apparently was acceptable in May for correcting this situation is no longer acceptable in November. The minister could only repeat the words of the secretary of the Treasury Boad. The Treasury Board secretary is the boss. Apparently that civil servant is the spokesman for the Treasury Board and he said what the minister will have to do.
Instead of acting on the horror stories contained in the Auditor General's report and getting rid of half a dozen men who made the mistakes or should have been held responsible for them, the government set up a royal commission. But this royal commission blew apart when it became evident that one or more of its members could be in an embarrassing position if there were an investigation. That being the case, how can the government bring before this House Bill C-19, the ostensible purpose of which is to restrain expenditure and refuse even while this bill is being debated to take advantage of the recommendations contained in the Auditor General's report whereby tremendous amounts of money could be saved? We are talking of tens of millions of dollars in savings.

Instead of talking about possible action, ministers stand up here like trained parrots and suggest, "We cannot touch the civil service." Who runs Canada? Is it the Treasury Board? At this moment of our history the ministers of this government have sided with the mandarins. They are protecting their fellow
November 26, 1976

mandarins. Who are these people, anyway? Three or four names keep popping up nearly all the time.
The hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) brought to the fore the Sky Shops affair, one name kept popping up in connection with Sky Shops. Then there is the question of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. One of the brightest things Canadian scientists have done is develop the CAN DU nuclear device which will provide electricity more efficiently and cleanly than any other similar device in the world. Its merit alone will spread it around the world as one of the main devices for producing electricity from nuclean fission; yet this fine development is covered with the slime of what we heard this past week.
That this government should condone agencies of government doing around the world what Lockheed did is an awful indictment of the moral levels to which this government has descended. I understand why the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) does not want to discuss these questions. He refuses to admit that the people of Canada are concerned about these matters. He thinks that as long as the government is called Liberal, no matter how wasteful it is the people will return it to power. He is ready to believe that because it has happened time and again. But one week ago Monday the people of the province of Quebec gave us hope that this will change when they threw out that corrupt government which was part and parcel of the corrupt government we have here.

So I say to
this government, do not ask us to pass a bill which would destroy one of the foundations of our federal system, our agreement to bind Canada together into one nation with railways and other forms of communication. Do not ask us to pass this bill at the very time you are refusing to take advice from anyone on how to save money and restrain waste.
For the foregoing reasons and others, we have proposed the amendment for hoisting the bill for six months. Hopefully during that six months the government will act on those basic problems raised by the Auditor General and by many members of this House during the last three or four years. That is my first point. Second, if we are to put our house in order we must restore to parliament its ancient right of having some say over the voting of money. I know that some intellectuals who got together ten years ago to change the rules now admit they were wrong. It is time for those intellectuals to confer again, to straighten out the rules and to give back to parliament some control over the administration. The first step must be to bring estimates back for consideration in parliament.
Third, a responsible government must hold senior civil servants accountable. Since we turned certain powers over to our civil servants, if in the spending of billions of dollars they make mistakes they must pay the price which all high-salaried people must pay when they make mistakes. Such a civil servant, if he makes a mistake, must go down the road; or, if you prefer a more Christian type of punishment, do hard labour. I hope the backbenchers of this government will dupli-
Restraint of Government Expenditures cate what the backbenchers of Japan did last spring. When their Prime Minister was exposed on account of all the activities of Lockheed in that country and the bribery of officials and business leaders, it was the backbenchers of the governing party in Japan who forced their Prime Minister to resign and go into the wilderness. That is what backbenchers are for. Stand up and be counted as representing the people of Canada and not just the voices of a few people in the cabinet who say you have to be good boys and applaud if you want to be promoted some day. Recognize that we all stand in the same position and that cabinet does not run the government.
They are being run by the same group of people who will want to run the next government that takes over. Sooner or later the ordinary members of this House will have to use their muscle, which is their votes, and throw out their Prime Ministers and leaders if they do not take on the responsibility which is theirs, and that is to govern and not be run by a group of technocrats, bureaucrats, and whatever you want to call them. That is the issue.
If the government wants to save money there is a lot of evidence on how to do that. However, do not ask this House to put through a bill that under the pretense of saving money breaks up the original agreements of Confederation. Once you start on that slope, there is no such thing as honour among the group of colleagues who now make this nation.
I want to conclude by saying let us give this bill a six months hoist. Let us hope that the awful headlines that shock us can disappear from our papers. I do not think there is a Canadian who did not see this morning's Globe and Mail which was headlined "Foreign Firms Bribed by Canada".
Today we have had the letter of the Prime Minister. He said to his senior ministers-Drury, Turner, Goyer, Sharp-"O.K. boys, get together and get this thing quieted down."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a very serious debate from the point of view that somehow or other Canadians expect us to get our House in order. They expect us to set an example and give them leadership on how they should pare their own budgets and live in a less extravagant style than the government has been personifying in recent years.
The proliferation of spending by government departments is shocking to the sensibilities of every taxpaying Canadian. As parliamentarians we must put the reins on Ottawa mandarins or else this country will be the closest thing to bankruptcy that any country can face.
The reason we are faced with inflation in this country more than any other country is because of the open ended spending by all government departments and Crown corporations.
There appears to be no need for the grandiose thoughts of the civil service in general, and the top echelon in particular with regard to spending more and more of the taxpayers' money day in and day out. I am sure that the empire building is repulsive to all members of parliament.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Rather than facing up to the facts laid before it by the Auditor General, the government appoints another royal commission. It will spend more money and allow more empire building while trying to find the reasons why there should be restraint, and the methods by which it can be accomplished. The government should not need a royal commission to determine that there is obviously a great deal of overspending in most government departments.
Year after year the Auditor General's report contains specific examples of departments spending as though it were going out of style. Yet whoever heard of a deputy minister or an assistant deputy minister being fired because of extravagance in running a department? Unfortunately one of the facts of life is that a government which has been in office as long as this one, a government which changes ministers around as often as this one, gets itself into a position where the individual deputy minister has more power than the minister. Portfolios are changed around, as if in a game of musical chairs, in an attempt to produce a new image for the government, but the only result is that the departments are bigger spenders than ever because of the weakness of ministers who assume duties about which they know nothing.
We in Atlantic Canada have suffered the tortures of the damned because of the culpability of the government in ignoring our legitimate aspirations to a better way of life. I should like to give an example of what happens when a government has run its course for a long period and then takes direction from mandarins based in Ottawa, people who have no idea of what is happening in the rest of the nation apart from what they dream up in their ivory towers and impose on those who live in the outer provinces.
In Nova Scotia we have seen money spent wastefully over and over again on projects which produce nothing for us except the ill will of other Canadians because plans conceived in Ottawa and sent down to us proved unworkable. They did not work because there had been no input in decision-making or planning at the local level. A project ends up as a failure, and instead of the mandarins in Ottawa being identified as the reason for the failure, people in the rest of the nation point a finger at us and say "You cannot do anything for them because nothing you do for them works; they will not make it work." Yet it was unworkable from the beginning, the reason being that officials here never took the trouble to seek advice locally as to whether it would work in the first place.
The best example is the record of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. There is no doubt that the government has committed many millions of dollars to various projects in the legitimate hope that the projects would improve the way of life of the people in our region. But once again the civil servants here conceived the ideas and said to us, "This is what is available for you; this is what you must do."

speechtext:
The money is spent without regard for local opinion. The projects are unsuccessful, and after the investment of millions of dollars the rate of employment is unchanged-we face the same lack of opportunity; we have the same bleak future to look forward to. This situation has to change.
The government could spend a lot less money in Atlantic Canada while deriving much greater benefit from the funds expended, provided the administration would consider projects which we in eastern Canada believe to be workable and likely to give us hope for tomorrow. The government must learn to accept the advice of their own people, the elected people, those who really know what is needed. The sooner it does this the earlier we shall eliminate the kind of attitude expressed by Rene Levesque, one which finds a following because the legitimate aspirations of the electorate have not been met and because of their frustration with governments which are not meeting their commitments. If the government were to decide to do what the people want done, it would be a lot cheaper and a great deal more effective in overcoming regional disparity.
For a long time Canadians across the country have been saying there should be a national power grid, and that if there were such a grid many hundreds of millions of dollars could be saved in the transmission and conservation of electricity. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), who spoke before me, was a forerunner, along with the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), in putting forward the concept of a national power grid to meet the anticipated energy crisis we are now facing. Way back in 1959 the Diefenbaker administration moved forward with this concept in mind. But in 1978 we shall be no further forward in the development of a national power grid than we are today. For 19 years there has been no real progress in achieving something which is realistic, sensible, and valuable to all Canadians no matter where they live. That is just one of many examples.
We in Atlantic Canada have been saying to governments since time immemorial that we want public works projects which are self-liquidating and which will give us the opportunity to develop our resources so that our people might have the option either to remain in the area or go somewhere else if they so desire. Today they have no option. They must go somewhere else if they are to hope to achieve their legitimate aspirations and make an optimum contribution to this nation.
For some 15 years I have been making speeches at every opportunity on the development of Fundy tidal power. I have done so because the harnessing of the Fundy tides would be a tremendous boost not just for the Atlantic provinces but for the whole nation. We in Atlantic Canada would be making a contribution that would be of benefit to other provinces if a national power grid were established. The only reply we have had from the government is the carrot on the stick before the donkey. We have had one study after the other.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
All that Fundy tidal power has produced so far is a very good life for some consultants who happen to be friends of the government in office. One study has been met by another study, followed by yet another study. We in Atlantic Canada have had layers of studies. If we could eat paper we would be the best fed people in the nation. I suggest there have been more studies made of the problems in Atlantic Canada than in the rest of the nation ever since Confederation.
Right now, Mr. Speaker, we are in the process of going through a third study on Fundy tidal power. When the first study was brought down it reported, in effect, that Fundy tidal power was engineeringly feasible but economically unrealistic. There was such an uproar at this in Atlantic Canada that the government finally agreed to conduct another study. This second study was more realistic. The carrot on the stick was not quite so far away from the donkey, but the donkey was still plodding along trying to reach the unattainable carrot. That study found that if tidal power were harnessed it would be competitive with oil at $10 a barrel. At that time oil was not $10 a barrel, Mr. Speaker; I think it was $8.50.
All of a sudden the government said that this study deserved another study. The third study is a lot fancier because it is phased. In recent days we had the report on the first phase of the third study. Probably by the time we are through we will have as many chapters and verses on studies of tidal power as there are chapters and verses in the Bible. The first phase report of the third study now says that if oil rises to $22 a barrel by 1983, tidal power will be competitive.
How we got from $10 to $22 a barrel is not explained. Construction costs and inflation being what they are, this figure is quite significant especially in view of the cost of producing power at either James Bay or at Wreck Cove in Nova Scotia. Even with firm contracts the price of the Wreck Cove hydro project has jumped from $90 million to $140 million. When you can escalate the cost of a project by $50 million under firm contracts, it is pretty good going, but this is typical of the kind of "firmness" that results from most of the consulting expertise that we have received in study reports in recent years in Atlantic Canada.
By the time the second phase is completed we will probably be told that Fundy tidal power will be feasible if the cost of oil rises to $30 a barrel by 1985; or we will be told some other fairy tale of similar type. If we had undertaken to produce power from the tides of Fundy when the first report in 1969 was completed, as they did in France with La Ranee, today we would have power pumping into a maritimes grid which would be competitive with the present cost of power, and probably would be a good deal cheaper. We would also have something else, Mr. Speaker. We would have an assured supply of energy, something that we do not have at the present time. Indeed today we are captives of the OPEC nations, and we all know it. Unfortunately this government and the government of Nova Scotia have gotten themselves in a mess by committing themselves to an energy economy based on what is now very expensive oil.
