If the government wants to know how to restrain its expenditures, one way to do so is by firing half of the consultants it has on contract at the present time, including those studying Fundy tidal power, and by calling tenders to build the actual project. I am not necessarily saying they should build at all three sites at the same time.
If the government wants to improve its engineering expertise, I suggest it build the smallest of the three sites, Cumberland Basin, which would cost approximately $1.2 billion but which, when completed, would guarantee a source of supply for the next 75 years, thus giving protection to the people of Atlantic Canada against power shortages in the future. That is point No. 1. Point No. 2 is that this project would provide much needed employment and would result in such spin-off effects as a fantastic increase in tourism. This would be associated with the desire of people to see the mightiest public works venture ever undertaken in this country, in an area that is completely accessible to everybody here and in the United States who might want to come and see what Canada is doing for its people.
That is the kind of project that makes sense. It would be an investment in the future of Canada. It would be a guarantee of a new tomorrow for Canadians. It would make Canadians believe there is some realism in the minds of the people running the government of this country. Such a realism escapes the thoughts of people these days when they see the kind of headlines that appear, talking about corruption and the like, in respect of the operations of the Government of Canada. Restraint in respect of stupid things would produce the dollars to undertake the realistic things that Canadians want and which would be of benefit to them and of benefit to this nation in its totality.
The sooner we start moving down that road the sooner we will eliminate the talk of separatism, the talk of disenchantment, and the talk of who cares whether we are or are not a nation, which is in the minds of so many Canadians today. We must have a common objective for all Canadians regardless of where they may live. We must have the belief that there is something worth while about this nation that we should work toward.
You know, Mr. Speaker, it is pretty unrealistic that one could come to the conclusion that a nation could break up because some people who speak the French language do not desire to speak the English language, and some people who speak the English language do not desire to speak the French language. This is particularly true when we look at a nation like Israel which is composed of people from all over the world who speak many different languages, and many different dialects of language, people who have come together and who have remained together under the greatest kind of adversity that exists in the world, and yet who are able to marshal to the cause because they have a common objective and a common goal which they all wish to attain.
[Mr. Coates.)
Surely we on the northern half of this North American continent, regardless of the language we speak, have a common goal not only to make this nation and the people who live in it better, but to make the world a better place in which to live because of the tremendous resources God has given us in the northern half of this continent.
Surely we can find in the leadership of this nation the ability to set standards which are high enough that all Canadians can see something in Canada that will make them want to come together, work together, live together, and achieve together. Surely we are not getting that today. This is one reason for the erosion we see and feel in respect of the Confederation of Canada. The government could do much to overcome and eliminate the problems we have today if it would set that high standard, look at the leadership that is being given economically and otherwise, say to Canadians that there is more that is good about this country than there is that is bad, let us work together as Canadians to make it a better place for all of us to live in regardless of where we may live, and say to Canadians that it is important we do this because if we live and live well we can make life a lot better for many other Canadians, and for many other people who live on this earth in other parts of the world by sharing with them some of the things we have in abundance.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND OR REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES TO ENABLE RESTRAINT OF GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is yet another opportunity to participate in the discussion in respect of Bill C-19, a bill designed to give effect to government restraint in spending programs. I take pleasure in supporting the amendment that is now before us to the effect that we not now read this bill a second time but rather do something else with it for six months instead of continuing with this madness on the part of the government.
For the next few minutes I intend to concentrate again on clause 15 of this bill which relates to the repeal of section 272 of the Railway Act, dealing with what we now fondly refer to as the "at and east'' grain and flour rates. It has become obvious that the government, hoping to find time to formulate a legislative program for this fall which might show some kind of leadership and some direction for the country, has in fact brought in Bill C-19 containing this controversial clause as nothing more than a stalling tactic to get around its responsibility to govern and give direction to Canada.
Much has been said this afternoon in respect of the degree of restraint that would be achieved by this bill. Let me reiterate what we are talking about with regard to this bill which the government says will do so much, and which it holds up as its great shield in the fight against spending. The government intends to take away the subventions on the movement of grain and flour to the extent this year of, I think, very close to $13 million or $14 million, and yet the government very clearly has before it a recommendation which I assume has cabinet approval, the effect of which would be to establish a program of assistance for Canadian milling operations equal to the money to be saved by the removal of the subsidy in respect of the so-called "at and east" rates on grain.
November 26, 1976

Where is the saving? What the government is doing is taking the money away from the railways and giving it to the millers.
I do not argue against the justness of the plea on the part of the Canadian milling operators for this assistance because they have to compete with foreign countries for the export flour trade. We all know that the European countries heavily subsidize their milling operations for this very specific purpose. 1 am not arguing against that. What 1 am asking is, of what earthly good is it to take it out of one pocket and put it in another? Where is the restraint in spending in that?
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is trying to achieve his avowed intention to remove all forms of subsidy from the varying transport modes in Canada, despite the still existent government policy that transportation should be used in the development of this country for the proper location of people, to assist people in their settlement in various areas of the country, and for the transportation of goods between them. All this will achieve is to push the Minister of Transport a little farther down the road toward his avowed goal of removing transport subsidies, but it does not save the taxpayer one nickel.
Indeed, as I understand it, the government intends to give to millers an amount of money equal to the compensation paid to the railway. Presumably that compensation in the years ahead would be geared as well to the continuing difference that would exist between the real cost of moving grain and flour and the subsidized rate set in 1960 with respect to flour, just for example. I see no dollar saving futures for the Canadian taxpayer in that. What dollars were saved by bringing the Company of Young Canadians to an end? What dollars were saved by Information Canada, a useless body? This bill does not do what the government purports it will accomplish, and to continue to insist that it does is to mislead the Canadian people.
Let us come back to clause 15 of the bill to see what the social and economic costs to the Atlantic provinces will be if we remove that particular subsidy. If there is any reason for Bill C-19 being in front of us, it is, 1 suppose, to exasperate those who want to get on with measures that are meaningful and useful to the country. If the bill's principal purpose is to frustrate the opposition and frustrate Canadians and put them in positions of confrontation, then it does succeed, and that is regrettable in the sense that we should be doing things to give renewed direction to Canada. I intend, as I said in this debate two days ago, and as I said last spring, to do everything in my capacity and within my abilities to make sure that Bill C-19 does not pass so long as it includes clause 15. For me or for anyone else from the Atlantic provinces to do less, I think, would be to perform a great disservice to the people in the area they represent, and I do not intend to do that.
The deletion of Section 272 from the Railway Act could not come at a worse time for Atlantic Canada currently facing a totally unacceptable unemployment rate and one which, if we listened to OECD, will get worse unless drastic measures are
Restraint of Government Expenditures taken now. For example, energy rates in Nova Scotia are increasing rapidly. Oil, for which we pay $1.75 a barrel until the end of next month, will increase to $12 or $13 a barrel. Who knows what it will go to? Energy rates will go up 65 per cent immediately, which is totally unacceptable to the people. Rates that are already well above those in all other parts of the country except Prince Edward Island, will rise substantially. There is no question that our energy problems will have a serious and long term detrimental effect on the development of the economy of our region. My colleague, the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates), has spoken about the great potential of the Fundy tides. He is right when he says we should have been developing that program ten years ago. Not to do so within the next two or three years will again be a major disservice to our region.
Late last night we were discussing the shipbuilding and repair industry which in the maritime provinces directly employs thousands of people, and indirectly many more thousands. That industry is in its most depressed state in more than a decade. On top of all this was the recent turn of events in the province of Quebec. I fear-and I hope my fears are groundless-that this could very well cause a serious slowdown in economic investment in Atlantic Canada, and this is to be regretted.
While it has been the federal government's response to the plight of Atlantic Canada to put forward a program designed to combat chronic unemployment in Canada, has the government offered special assistance to energy consumers to help offset high rate increases? Has it increased subsidies for shipbuilding or announced any programs for ship construction to complement our announced intention with regard to surveillance of the 200 mile limit, and the development of underwater resources? Has it assured potential investers in the Atlantic region that their capital is as secure there as in any area of Canada?
I appreciate the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) remarks on television the other night, but they will not persuade the economic institutions to invest their dollars in Atlantic Canada. It is deeds and actions on the part of the government that will achieve that, not the bland assurances of a government which tricked us in 1970 with smooth words and sweet talk on the crisis in Quebec. We swallowed it. We believed it. We sat in this Chamber and voted for a War Measures Act that was not necessary, only because the people of Canada were persuaded by a great performer, by words and the television medium. We were tricked then. We were tricked with A1B by a smooth talker. I tell you, the people of Canada will not be fooled by what he said the other night. Rather, they will only be convinced by action and deeds and if the government restores their confidence in itself.
The great tragedy today is that nobody in this country believes in the federal government. They cannot trust it. Let us consider Bill C-61. There are some flaws in it but it is not a bad bill. Nobody would accept it. The Minister of Transport could not get that bill through the House on his own terms, not

November 26, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures even if he used closure. Why? Because no matter what he says, nobody will believe him, and why should they?
No, it will take actions, not words, from this government before the people of Canada will give back to this institution their trust and give back to those who serve here some of the honour which has been stripped away from us by the Prime Minister and his colleagues on the treasury benches.
The government has not done anything for us yet. Instead it has attempted to shove down our throats and the throats of Maritimers a bill, the immediate impact of which will be to cause the loss of hundreds and hundreds of jobs. This immediate loss of employment will occur at two Maritime ports, Saint John and Halifax, if the "at and east" rates are removed. Let us not kid ourselves; they simply cannot be competitive in grain and flour export traffic without this rate. They will not be competitive, through no fault on their own, but only because preferential treatment has been given to other trading routes. I am also under the clear impression that the government qualified this to say it will not extend any subsidy to any flour which would move through a U.S. trading route, and I hope that that is in fact the case.
Let us see what this means in calculable dollar and cent terms to the port of Halifax-Dartmouth and to the port of Saint John, New Brunswick. I ask hon. members to remember that the port of Halifax is still struggling as a result of a lengthy port dispute which cost us millions and millions of dollars and from which we have not as yet fully recovered. If section 272 of the Railway Act is repealed, the port of Halifax-and I will deal with Halifax and then Saint John and try to sum it up later-will lose 210,000 man-hours with regard to the handling of flour alone. That figure is based on the 1975 figures pro rated to 1977. This, plus the loss of 45 elevator jobs and 5 others in grain handling, will result in a loss to employees in terms of income, wages and benefits of an amount well in excess of $2 million annually.
These figures do not include jobs which would be lost at the port in such areas as administration of the dock employees, port agency staff, pilots, clerks, policing activities, private security arrangements and so on.
The loss to the port of Saint John is just as serious if not more so.

He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-203 has been around the Parliament of Canada for quite a while. It was first presented to the Twenty-Ninth Parliament as Bill C-377 by the present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson), who is and was then the hon. member for York North. As I have seen the destructive effect of present legislation on human beings many times in my life in service to the community, and as I made in 1972, and again in 1974, an election platform commitment to support that bill, I went to the hon. member for York North, who became a minister of the Crown in the Thirtieth Parliament, and asked if I could resubmit the principle of his bill to this parliament. The hon. gentleman agreed and gave me his blessing, and here we are two years later with the privilege of discussing this important subject matter in this parliament.
Somewhere, somehow, there has to be a person who can express in other than legal terms the plight of adults, and particularly of young people who have been caught in the ever increasing social malaise of family breakdown in Canadian society. The introduction of this private member's bill is an attempt to draw attention to this matter and to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) to use the power of his office, and the responsibility given to him by the people of
Alimony and Maintenance
Canada, to correct the rising level of anguish which is affecting the quality of life and the future of many Canadians.
I am a layman, and I realize that in true legal terms we are dealing with a division of legal powers pertaining to marriage and/or family breakdown, the federal legal responsibility being for alimony orders granted at the time of the divorce decree. I realize also that the provincial legal responsibility is for maintenance orders from the time of the separation to the time the divorce decree is granted. But, Mr. Speaker, some way, somehow, we have to find a way out of this constitutional and legal jungle if we are to reduce the growing number of family and human tragedies in this country. To continue with an abdication of our responsibility in this area of social need is to abandon any further move toward true justice in society.
The government is obviously aware of this social-human problem for it has commissioned study upon study on the subject. All that can really be said has already been printed. 1 should like to quote from the most recent study paper done by the Law Reform Commission, again at the request of the federal government. The paper is entitled "Family Law Enforcement of Maintenance Orders", and extracts are as follows:
A court order for maintenance of a dependent spouse or child is for all practical purposes often worth no more than the paper it is written on.
I quote again:
The rules, practices and procedures that exist in Canada for ensuring that support obligations are met following a marriage breakdown or divorce are the weakest links in the legal chain that comprises family law.
I quote again from that paper:
The primary federal interest in maintenance obligations and their enforcement stems from parliament's occupation in 1968 of the legislative field of family maintenance following divorce. Parliament has a clear responsibility to ensure that orders made pursuant to its legislation for the support of children and the economically weaker spouse are more than empty gestures. In addition to maintenance of a spouse and of children of a marriage-are matters historically associated with the status of marriage, a subject matter falling within the legislative competence of parliament under the Canadian constitution. For many years parliament has been inactive with respect to the exercise of such legislative powers as it possesses in this area.
Another quote from that paper is as follows:
The enforcement of the federally-created maintenance obligation on divorce is often done by provincial courts employing provincial law.
The federal government, Mr. Speaker, has been sloughing off leadership and action and its responsibilities to the provinces. If 1 may quote again from the report:
Jurisdiction questions should be distinctly secondary to finding appropriate answers.
As a layman, Mr. Speaker, impatient with the legal jurisdictional jungle, I am aware that maintenance and alimony orders from the courts of Canada are being abused. Contempt for the justice system is enhanced because of this enforcement breakdown and apparent refusal of the Department of Justice to accept its full social responsibility.
In support of this harsh challenge I offer a few statistics. The Vancouver Family Court reports that for the month of

November 26, 1976
Alimony and Maintenance
June, 1976, 65 per cent of receipts due under orders were received, leaving a failure to pay rate of 35 per cent. In March of the same year, the failure to pay rate was 42 per cent. In cases where the earning spouse who has received an order from the British Columbia courts has moved away from that provincial jurisdiction, the 1972 statistics show a failure to enforce rate of 72 per cent. We have had trouble updating these statistics, and I might add that Vancouver appears to be one of the few areas keeping a record that is available.
These figures are further confirmed by a statement in a letter from the assistant deputy minister of social allowances and services, Department of National Health and Welfare, as follows:
Some degree of default with respect to obligations arising under maintenance orders occurs in as many as 75 per cent of all maintenance orders.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the anxiety and destruction of spirit that must exist for people and children living under these conditions? People without hope or a goal are people missing out on a fair chance at the excitement of life.
According to the Law Reform Commission Report on Alimony and Maintenance, there are many factors causing the non-payment syndrome. Some factors are federal and some are provincial, and some overlap these legislative jurisdictions.
The present federal Divorce Act and the provincial Deserted Wives and Children's Maintenance Acts foster alienation between the partners in the procedures used are fault oriented and accusatory. The spouses are polarized through accusations and counter accusations because the "legal fault" affects the award they will receive. In most cases the legal fault or innocence is far removed from the actual cause of the marriage breakdown. Because of these procedures the spouses having to pay the order see the order as having been imposed on them because they are the bad person in the relationship- not because they should bear the responsibility for supporting their family. This resentment is in many cases the reason for non-payment.
Section 4(1 )(c) of the Divorce Act seems to provide a way to avoid the painful process of the accusatory procedures. Divorce is allowed after three years of legal separation. However, on careful scrutiny we note that it promotes the disassociation of the partners. Only 90 days of cohabitation are allowed for reconciliation and if that period should last for longer before they separate again, the entire three year separation must begin again from the start. Judges have also been known to refuse a divorce because the partners had seen each other too often. This disassociation of spouses causes children to lose interest in the parent who is not living with them. This again leads to non-payment, in that the parent feels that if the children do not care, why should they?
The quasi-criminal nature of enforcement proceedings may involve putting a defaulter in jail using procedures prescribed by the Criminal Code. These very harsh measures have caused spouses who have fallen into arrears due to real financial difficulties to fear the court, and such people will allow arrears to pile up rather than consult the court with their problem.

The present system is designed to involve lawyers, and because of their cost people are reluctant to use their services. On the other hand lawyers are reluctant to get involved because it is time-consuming and there is no money in it. An extract from a bar admission course on enforcement of periodic maintenance orders confirms this as follows:
There is no money in maintenance enforcement from the point of view of the solicitor-it is time-consuming, frustrating and often engenders ill-will from your client when she is charged a fee that she considers exorbitant but is still less than your time is worth.
A new system must be developed that does not depend entirely on the services of the legal profession in this area of need. Welfare payments also tend to promote non-payment; deserted spouses often prefer welfare because payments are regular. Another factor is the seemingly permanent nature of maintenance orders which is said to be psychologically discouraging. A lump sum arrangement should be considered.
The garnisheeing of wages of the spouse who is paying the maintenance is rarely considered. The legal procedures and the administration and bookkeeping involved on the part of the employer are such that garnisheeing is not feasible. Many times the employer would rather get rid of the employee than get involved in these procedures. Judges are also extremely reluctant to place defaulters in prison. The defaulters may lose their jobs and would therefore not be able to pay at all.
The lowest success rate in enforcing alimony and manite-nance orders occurs when a spouse leaves the provincial jurisdiction of the deserted partner. The interprovincial enforcement of alimony and maintenance orders is almost impossible, even when reciprocal agreements exist between the provinces. The low success rate is in part due to the varying provincial statutes relating to maintenance orders and procedures involving the finding and summonsing of the deserting spouse. This is time consuming and costly, and more often than not results in non-payment anyway in that the spouse cannot be traced. On the other hand the spouse, if found, could be having financial problems and only has to prove this fact to the court. The spouse may be then relieved of responsibility.
Increasing welfare costs surely dictate a move on the part of the federal government toward the co-ordination of collection procedures. It has been reported to me by a reliable source that 80 per cent of welfare costs in the city of Vancouver not attributable to senior citizens, are caused by deserted women with children. I am sure that other Canadian cities would show similar statistics. Such welfare cost burdens are shared equally by federal and provincial jurisdictions.
In any study to resolve this problem one must take note of the successes being experienced by the Ontario automatic enforcement program which has also been supplemented with their parental support program. 1 would think that the experience gained under these two programs in the province of Ontario would be useful and is essential if there is to be action on the part of the federal government in this serious area of social need.
November 26, 1976

As I approach my conclusion I can do no better than quote again from the Law Reform Commission paper on family law. I quote paragraph (m) on page 941. The paragraph is headed "Uniform Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Legislation". It reads in part:
Since many of the possible solutions to present problems involve interprovincial issues as well as federal-provincial matters, consideration should be given to a co-operative approach among the provinces and between the provinces and the federal government with a view to uniform provincial legislation embodying new enforcement techniques, coupled with new federal legislation complementing the action taken by the provinces. Such an approach is closely connected with the creation of the unified family court.
As 1 have become more involved in the technical considerations of studies made since presenting this bill for first reading, I fully realize that the bill is a broad and simplistic attempt to resolve a serious and complicated social problem. I can only hope that this debate on the principle of the bill will once again bring an awareness to the federal government that leadership and legislation are urgently needed to reduce the degree of emotional warping of both parents and children, and to reduce the long-lasting social damage and costs that present legislative indifference encourages. Again 1 ask the government to approve Bill C-203, especially in light of apparent federal government concern that new legislation in the area of marriage and family law is past due.
To close my remarks may 1 put on record the explanatory note concerning this bill. It reads:
In the eyes of many people, deserting spouses in default of alimony and maintenance orders are a blight on our society who are aided and abetted by the costly and timely procedures under the various provincial statutes respecting the reciprocal enforcement of these orders. This bill, which purports to establish with the approval of all the provinces, an agency to enforce in one province alimony and maintenance orders issued in another, is admittedly only a first step. It is hoped that from this bill will flow a government measure providing for the automatic and guaranteed payment of alimony and maintenance orders awarded by the court, and for the federal and provincial governments to be responsible for collecting these payments.

subsubtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE ORDER ENFORCEMENT ACT SUGGESTED AGENCY TO ENFORCE COURT ORDERS
speechtext:
The purpose of the bill is to establish a federal-provincial agency to enforce in one province alimony and maintenance orders issued in another. It would, in effect, make the federal and provincial governments jointly responsible for the collection of payments under these orders. What would such an agency do and where would it be located? If the agency were only used as a data and tracing centre, possibly one national office would suffice. However, even as a tracing service one would expect that at least one office in each province would be necessary.
Further, if the agency were to go beyond tracing and attempt to provide an effective enforcement service, the agency would probably have to have offices not only in every province but also in at least several areas of nearly every province. It would have to hire investigative officers to trace missing persons against whom maintenance orders had been issued, and to investigate the means of such persons to pay orders. It would also have to hire enforcement officers to enforce the orders where a person refused or neglected to pay. If these procedures were handled purely automatically, it would be a very rigid system and would probably result in many people who could not pay their debts being sent to jail or forced to suffer other penalties.
For any system of enforcement to work there must be an opportunity for judicial review. It is pointless to enforce an order against a person who has no money to pay. If there is to be a judicial review to ascertain whether orders should or can be enforced, then any agency created to perform this function would in effect be a court. If a special federal court were created to perform this function, it is highly likely that the provinces, with considerable justification, would object strongly on the grounds that the creation of the court was an infringement of the administration of justice in the provinces. There are already provincial courts in existence that are engaged in the enforcement of maintenance orders. It would seem preferable to strengthen the enforcement function in existing court structures, or in new unified family court structures, rather than to try to create a new agency to handle the problem.
1442

November 26, 1976
Alimony and Maintenance
The enforcement of maintenance orders is an important element in the administration of justice in the family law field. The scheme of reciprocal enforcement is grafted upon provincial enforcement in the province where a maintenance order is confirmed or registered. As a result, no scheme of reciprocal enforcement will be able to operate any better than the provincial procedures to be applied in the endorsement of all maintenance obligations in the province.
The question of how to achieve more effective enforcement of maintenance orders has been considered by a number of authorities. They stress the importance of not only uniformity of substantive law but also uniformity of procedure in legal institutions. The Ontario commissioners, in a report to the Uniform Law Conference of Canada Annual Meeting, 1976, expressed the view that most problems, not only of inter, but also intra-enforcement of maintenance orders, would best be solved by vesting jurisdiction over all family matters in a single unified family court. This view reflects similar views expressed by the Law Reform Commission of Canada in its report on family law issued last June.
In order to provide an effective national enforcement scheme, it is necessary not only to have uniformity throughout the country but also to have automatic enforcement whereby the court rather than the recipient of the order is responsible for the enforcement of the order. If a maintenance order is not paid, then a wife and children often require welfare payments. The state then, as well as the person being maintained by the state, is directly interested in enforcing the maintenance order. The automatic enforcement of maintenance orders has other beneficial effects. It discourages the accrual of arrears which form a psychological barrier to future compliance with the order. Also, the regular review of performance under the orders often discloses factual situations that would justify applications to vary the orders. It is submitted that only a court, not a government agency can maintain the supervision necessary to ensure that the order is enforced in a manner fair to both parties.
Recognition of the necessity for the state to enforce maintenance orders has already led the courts in several provinces to experiment with automatic enforcement programs. The provinces of Alberta, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Manitoba and Ontario all have some system of court enforcement under development or in operation. Under the Ontario program enforcement proceedings no longer await the initiative of the welfare administration or the spouse in whose favour the order is made, usually the wife. Maintenance accounts are reviewed regularly, and as soon as an account appears to be in arrears, the defaulting spouse, usually the husband, is notified and asked to explain the default.
There is evidence, even at this date, that automatic enforcement schemes are effective. Indeed some of the current problems of the schemes are the result of their success. In some areas the system has become overloaded and appears to suffer from inadequate staffing. The result is that periodic review of the files can only take place at more infrequent intervals, which places the entire program in jeopardy. In order to
[Mr. Landers.)
prevent these schemes from faltering, it then becomes necessary to allocate more resources to them. However, in these days of financial constraint, both federal and provincial, the allocations of financial resources to new programs is difficult to accomplish.
The federal government, in an effort to improve the enforcement of maintenance orders along with other aspects of the administration of family law, is encouraging the provinces to establish unified family courts with effective support services by offering funds for cost-shared pilot projects. To this end the federal government has appropriated $400,000 for unified family court pilot projects for the 1976-77 fiscal year, and the same amount for the 1977-78 fiscal year. For various reasons none of these projects is yet operational.
In Manitoba approval in principle for a jointly funded unified family court pilot project within the County Court District of St. Boniface, was announced on July 18, 1976, by the Minister of Justice and the attorney general of Manitoba. Pursuant to provincial legislation now enacted, the St. Boniface Family Law Division will hear and determine all family law matters that arise in the district. The court will provide enforcement services. It was intended that the project commence operation November 1. However, the Manitoba government has requested the attorney general of that province to defer the starting date for the project until the fiscal year commencing April 1, 1977, for budgetary reasons.
The province of British Columbia unilaterally commenced a pilot project two years ago in the provincial family court. It provides a two-tier system, usually federally appointed judges, to hear divorces and other matters beyond the jurisdiction of provincially appointed judges. The Department of Justice has recently entered into an agreement with British Columbia under the unified family court pilot projects program to cost-share the evaluation work now being done on that unified family court pilot project. It is hoped that this evaluation will prove useful in respect of future family court pilot projects and programs.
In Ontario discussions have been held between the Minister of Justice and the attorney general of Ontario respecting the establishment of a unified family court pilot project in the Hamilton area. It is expected that agreement to proceed with this will soon be reached.
With regard to the other provinces, negotiations for a cost-sharing agreement with Saskatchewan were in an advanced stage when the province postponed the project for budgetary reasons. Some discussions have been held with other provinces but have not reached an advanced stage.
To say that the federal government is giving support to family court pilot projects is not to say that this is all that can be done by the federal government to facilitate the enforcement of maintenance orders. Every means of co-operation with the provinces should be and is being examined. In some cases, the means to promote the enforcement of maintenance orders may conflict with other social goals, such as the goal of ensuring privacy for persons in their transactions with the state. For example, in England the government has authorized
November 26, 1976

the disclosure of addresses from some official records to courts at their request. In the United States special units have been set up in state welfare departments to trace missing persons who are in breach of their support obligations. Legislation has been enacted in some states allowing departments to obtain from the records of other state agencies information which would assist in tracing individuals.

speechtext:
I am trying to take a global view rather than be parochial.
The development of facilities for the rapid and thorough exchange of information about persons, subject to suitable safeguards regarding the privacy of individuals involved, would greatly aid the effective enforcement of maintenance orders. Perhaps it is time that the social goal of ensuring privacy to individuals in respect of their dealings with the state be made subordinate to the goal of ensuring that parents who are able to do so support their children. In such a case is it time to open provincial and federal records to enable the tracing of people who do not comply with maintenance orders?
For tracing purposes at the provincial level the records of motor vehicle registration departments and hospital insurance agencies would be most useful. At the federal level, tax records, unemployment insurance records, and social insurance numbers would provide valuable information.
Given the conflicting social goals, the opening of these records for any purpose, even one as worthy as the one discussed here, is a matter which would have to be developed and worked out with the provinces over a period of time. It is also a matter which might require reference both to parliament and the provincial legislatures. It is not something which can be achieved over night through the creation of a new federal agency.
Taking into consideration the need for consultation and the necessity for maintaining close contacts with the courts in respect of the enforcement of maintenance orders, I would submit that the creation of a new and expensive federal-provincial agency, as suggested by this bill, is not the answer to the problem of how to provide an effective enforcement service. Rather, the answer lies in greater federal-provincial co-operation and the development of existing and new court systems and methods to meet this very real need.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say again what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said perhaps better than 1 can. This is a sensible and practical approach to a problem which has been imposing tremendous costs in every sense, fiscal, social and legal.
I note, looking over some of the material I am privileged to read, that the former minister of justice had this on his mind and that in reply to one of his constituents about this problem on May 7, 1975, he stated certain views. 1 see also that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) released a communique on this subject on June 18 recognizing the seriousness of the matter which has been brought up so well by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington).
1 was disturbed by what 1 considered to be an unnecessarily complicated and negative approach taken by the parliamentary secretary. As the previous speaker has just said, there is no reason why the bill should not be sent to the committee for further consideration and possible amendment. As one who has practised law 1 can testify that under the present circumstances everyone involved is unhappy with the situation as it now exists.
The federal government took the initiative some years ago to amend drastically the law on divorce. It now has a duty to go further and deal with the consequences which were implicit in those amendments and join with the law enforcement agencies in the provinces to find some acceptable way of enforcing what every lawyer now knows is practically unenforceable. Today, any person who is determined to avoid alimony payments can do so simply by moving to another province, and moving again if necessary. The cost to the country and to the people who are victimized is enormous. Apart from the additional welfare costs, one must also take account of increased social unhappiness and disrespect for the law. Neglect of this problem produces not a single desirable consequence.
To take the view that the bill is too complicated or insufficiently comprehensive to warrant consideration at this time is nonsense. The bill is one of the best which has been brought into the Chamber recently in private members' hour. It is the product of a bipartisan attempt by a minister of the Crown, representing an initiative conceived by him when he was a backbencher, and it is brought forward by the hon. member for Capilano who made a very perceptive speech in its support. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure to be able to add a few remarks to the debate this afternoon inasmuch as I, like the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), have had practical experience in attempting to pursue maintenance orders from the point of view of a practitioner of law. I do not, however, share the hon. member's dissatisfaction with the ability to pursue these matters quite to the extent that he does or seems to think the entire legal fraternity does.
It seems to me that with the assistance of legislation such as exists in the province of Ontario with the Reciprocal Enforcement of the Maintenance Orders Act-and I cannot but assume that the same type of legislation exists in many if not all of the other jurisdictions in Canada-the provincial jurisdiction has made a substantial attempt to provide mechanisms and agencies whereby maintenance order persons who attempt to get away from their obligations can be tracked down. I would advise the hon. member that with some satisfaction on a number of occasions I have successfully followed single time and double time movers. I am suggesting to you, Mr. Speaker, and to those persons across the way who obviously know not whereof they speak, that it is not particularly costly to do; that mechanisms have been set up which allow one to go through family courts and through the division courts, which are substantially less expensive than the other courts, to collect maintenance orders granted by the divorce courts which the federal jurisdiction set up just a few years ago.
To set up another agency and another level of courts would, I suggest, be foolhardy, and would add inordinate costs to a system which is already prepared and capable of handling the situation, with a few amendments. The State of Michigan, for instance, has a mechanism whereby through an agency called the Friend of the Court, maintenance orders can be deposited within the jurisdiction of the state in which a defaulting maintenance father or mother is located. The sheriff of the jurisdiction pays a visit to the individual and requires that he, under a warrant he has with him, show cause why he should not be put in jail immediately. I suggest that the effect of this has been substantial in that state, and in fact has substantially reduced the number of defaulters.

speechtext:
I suggest to hon. members who ask me whether or not I will be bringing this forward shortly that it cannot be brought forward under the type of legislation the principle of which is set out in this bill. If in fact the provincial jurisdictions accepted the responsibility vested in them and provided teeth for the family courts and collection agencies in their province to collect what can be collected before a family court in another jurisdiction, then we would not have the

problem we have at the present time. The difficulty is that provincial jurisdictions have not accepted their responsibility. In addition to that, might I suggest that they obviously recognize their responsibilities in legislation like the Reciprocal Enforcement of Maintenance Orders Acts. The problem is that we have not followed through. I suggest that it is at these levels that the following through should take place.
Hon. members opposite say there are problems here. A couple of nights ago their leader was talking of decentralization. They are now suggesting that another form of federalism should be applied so as to take away more powers from the provinces. 1 would really ask them just where they stand. If we are talking about decentralization and we really mean it, then let us give the leadership to bring the provinces together so as to provide the mechanism whereby maintenance orders can be collected. This is where the problem lies. The power should lie with the provinces, and it is there we say it should stay.
The hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) argued that a mechanism such as garnishee does not work. 1 suggest to hon. members that it not only works but it is the cheapest mechanism that is available. For instance in Ontario an order of the court either in the divorce jurisdiction or of the family court can simply be deposited with the division court at no cost. It is accepted at face value, and all the offices of the court are then brought to bear and made available to collect the amount. A garnishee order is simply sent forward with a stamp from the clerk of the division court to the employer, who is then bound by law to forward the funds.
To suggest that this procedure does not work, I put it to hon. members, is clearly wrong. Similarly it has been suggested that it might mean the loss of the job of the individual concerned. If the hon. member would pursue that he would find that although frequently this is suggested by the employer, who does not like being embroiled in all the paper work, the labour code of the various provincial jurisdictions of this country will not allow a person to lose his job for this reason. An employee would soon get his job back if ever his employer did try to take it away on that ground.
The hon. member brought up a number of valid points regarding the cost of the welfare system. He suggested that we do have a false system of divorce in this country at the present time and that there are motions afoot to have it changed. That fact is substantiated by the numerous changes that are being offered in legislation. For example, I understand that in its current session the province of Ontario is bringing forward new legislation in the field of family law. I submit that a recognition has taken place in that jurisdiction that there is an obligation to bring forward this kind of legislation.
To put into place a new series of courts, or another agency to do what the provincial courts can do now, seems to me to be a principle that is unacceptable at this time. Therefore in standing to speak on this matter I would suggest that I cannot support this principle. I think this is the wrong place; legislation should be brought forward at the provincial level, not here. I do not think that this bill deals with the issues advanced by the hon. member for Capilano, such as legal fault, deser-

subsubtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL ALIMONY AND MAINTENANCE ORDER ENFORCEMENT ACT SUGGESTED AGENCY TO ENFORCE COURT ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), a member I know and like very much. I was interested in his earnest plea that this very fine piece of legislation, as he described it, be sent to the justice committee for further consideration and amendment, so as to give an opportunity for something to be done in the complex and urgent area of reform of family law. However, I believe he neglected to listen carefully to his colleague, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), who indicated to the House, I thought in a magnanimous and forthright way, that he really was not offering parliament a solution to this complex problem but was merely opening up the subject for debate. He recognized that what he was putting forward was a band-aid solution, a small patch on a very complicated system that certainly needs reforming.
I think the hon. member for Capilano deserves to be commended for bringing this matter before the House, because in so doing he properly urges that the government with all due haste take action in the whole area of family law reform, which is something we all want. The parliamentary secretary correctly pointed out to the House that this is not an area where the federal government can move unilaterally; there has to be negotiation with the provinces. There has to be extensive consultation. It seems to me that this is the theme that the official opposition has been proposing all along as'being the approach in a federal system. The opposition has been saying that the federal government too often takes the high-handed approach, that it takes the leadership approach in solving
Alimony and Maintenance
national problems, and that we should talk more with the provinces. When we tell them, Mr. Speaker, that this takes a great deal of time, that it cannot be done overnight, they then protest that there is unnecessary delay. It seems to me that that is not an acceptable debating point at all.
In putting forward the proposal that we have this new agency established, the hon. member really has in mind one particular scenario. The scenario is that, on the one hand, we have a former partner in a marriage who is in desperate need. On the other hand we have a partner with the ability to pay who is not coming across with the dollars required under the maintenance order. The hon. member for Capilano indicated in his remarks that he recognizes this is part of a much larger question, namely, the economic readjustment on the dissolution of marriage. On that particular theme the Law Reform Commission has spent a great deal of time and has even come forward with a number of recommendations which could guide this government in its discussions with the provinces. Eventually I hope this will result in the kind of reform legislation the hon. member for Capilano and the hon. member for Central Nova say they want to see on the agenda.
I think it is well known that a marriage is not only a personal relationship but that it is also an economic arrangement. It is an essential aspect of the family unit that all who are not employed for wages must have their financial needs provided for. We begin with that principle. Then we know that it is a cultural fact, and usually a legal requirement as well, that men are the primary source of this financial provision. This means at the time of the divorce husbands have become owners of most of the property acquired during the marriage and are the ones who have a continuing maintenance obligation. The Law Reform Commission in its report on family laws addresses itself to this particular cultural aspect which has become enshrined in law, and challenges it, and suggests certain changes should be made in respect of that tradition.
Before 1968 divorce law in Canada assumed that a wife was always the financially dependent spouse. The old rules of maintenance provided a life income to a wife who was the "innocent" party in the divorce and punished the wife who was "guilty" by giving her nothing. That was the old law. The present law does not any longer assume the inherent dependency of women, but neither does it furnish any new rationale to replace the traditional reasons one spouse should continue to furnish money to the other after divorce has ended all other aspects of the relationship. There must of course always be some financial provision on dissolution of the marriage to meet the reasonable needs of the spouse who performed on behalf of both spouses family obligations which carry certain economic disadvantages.
We find so far as cash payments or alimony are concerned it is recommended in the Family Law Report that these should only be made during the time of transition from a period of dependency until the formerly dependent spouse is able to achieve a degree of self-sufficiency. The duration of the post-

That is why I say the hon. member for Capilano was thinking of a particular situation in which a spouse was not able to do that, and the other or former partner was in a strong position to meet those financial needs. There are many aspects in respect of which that is not the situation. The family law report addresses itself to those matters which are an equally important part of the larger problem referred to.

Dissolution. It goes on to say that the financial guarantee provided by law should be one of rehabilitation to overcome economic disadvantages caused by marriage, and not a guarantee of security for life for former dependent spouses. The obligation of the former spouse who is required to pay
should be balanced by the obligation of the other eventually to become self-sufficient, as are all other unmarried persons, within a reasonable period of time. 1 suppose that reasonable period of time would vary in all kinds of circumstances.
